policy: Preserve the named GRETIL transcription; correct import artifacts, attribution, and demonstrated draft errors. Comparisons do not constitute independent scholarly certification.

notes: The critical edition 1.16 has a substantially different list, including contentment and realization of truth. Correcting the isolated sandhi of the older transcription does not establish the critical reading. These edition differences must not be conflated.

The draft’s “recitation” interprets a reading japo, supported by the critical edition’s appended verse 1.16_2, against the repeated tapo in this transcription. This is an editorial interpretation, not a literal rendering of every transmitted syllable.
Sinh’s English says “hands”; the Sanskrit pāda-tale ubhe means “both soles”. The editorial draft follows the Sanskrit. The historical wording is retained with attribution.
Sanskrit Documents has gulkaṃ where GRETIL has gulphaṃ (ankle). This is a transcription difference; the atlas retains its named GRETIL base.
Sanskrit Documents has padmamāsanaṃ against GRETIL padmāsanaṃ. The extra syllable is not imported into the base text.
Sanskrit Documents has sīvantyāḥ against GRETIL sīvanyāḥ; compare the same difference at 1.55. Both displays need to be distinguished from independent manuscript evidence.
Sanskrit Documents has vyātta-vakto where GRETIL has vyātta-vaktro (with mouth open). The atlas retains the GRETIL reading.
Sanskrit Documents has sīvantyāḥ against GRETIL sīvanyāḥ. The Sinh English 55–57 crosses the Sanskrit 55–57 boundaries; shared text is repeated with its full English reference numbers.
Sanskrit Documents has bhavedsiddho against GRETIL bhavet siddho. This is a consonant-sandhi/spelling difference; the named GRETIL source is preserved.
Sanskrit Documents has kāla-bhayaṃ śrutaḥ where GRETIL has kāla-bhayaṃ kutaḥ. The latter gives the rhetorical question “whence fear of death?”; the alternative is recorded, not silently substituted.

Corrected the earlier draft’s “draw through the nose”: Sinh explicitly interprets the nasal action as expulsion. The critical edition discusses this as sītkārī at 2.54, with a different first half-verse.
2.54.draftTranslation: One should make a hissing sound at the mouth and exhale through the nose. Through this practice one becomes like a second god of love.

notes: Sanskrit Documents and the critical edition (2.69) support yogīndrāṇām against GRETIL’s corrupt yogīndrāṇī̀am. The draft uses that supported genitive plural; the source display remains diplomatic.
The historical English’s “carried down” reverses ūrdhvataḥ, “upward”. The snake comparison continues into 3.12; the draft now follows the Sanskrit verse boundary.
3.11.draftTranslation: Having applied a lock at the throat, one should hold the wind upward. Just as a snake struck with a stick takes the shape of a stick—

notes: Rendered separately from 3.11. The identification of the “two passages” with iḍā and piṅgalā is interpretive; the Sanskrit here does not explicitly say “leaves”.
3.12.draftTranslation: —so the power Kuṇḍalī suddenly becomes straight. Then she, resting in the two passages, enters a state like death.

notes: Removed a sentence belonging to the beginning of 3.14 that the historical English joins to its preceding verse.
3.13.draftTranslation: Then one should exhale very slowly, never forcefully. The foremost wise call this very technique mahāmudrā.

notes: Restored the opening clause and preserved the repeated mahāmudrā formula in this GRETIL verse. Other editions segment this passage differently.
3.14.draftTranslation: This mahāmudrā was demonstrated by the great adepts. Afflictions beginning with the great troubles and death diminish; for that very reason the foremost wise call it mahāmudrā.

notes: Replaced the historical English’s nostril-specific wording: candrāṅga and sūryāṅga describe sides or limbs in this posture context; nostrils are not specified.
3.15.draftTranslation: Having practised on the moon side, one should practise again on the sun side. When the counts on both sides are equal, one should release the mudrā.

notes: Sanskrit Documents writes prathamasādhanam continuously where GRETIL has prathama-sādhanam; the anusvāra/m difference is a word-final spelling distinction. The critical edition has a differently segmented passage at 3.30–31.

The older English “in 8 ways, daily and hourly” obscures the count and time unit. A yāma is a watch, conventionally about three hours, rather than one hour; the critical edition segments the concluding material differently.
3.31.draftTranslation: This is performed eight times in each watch, day after day, always bringing a store of merit and breaking the mass of wrongdoing. For those properly instructed, this is a modest initial practice.

notes: Corrected the mirror’s गी to the Sanskrit go and retained tālu as palate; “gullet” is an interpretive expansion in the historical English.
3.48.draftTranslation: The word go denotes the tongue; its insertion into the palate is “eating cow flesh”, which is said to destroy great wrongdoing.

notes: Corrected the historical English’s relocation of the sixteen-petalled lotus to the heart. The Sanskrit locates the falling stream at the head. The source’s ūrdvhāsyo is an apparent transposition; interpret as ūrdhvāsyo. This remains a draft of a difficult long stanza.
3.51.draftTranslation: With the face turned upward, restraining the tongue in the cavity and contemplating the supreme power, the yogin who drinks the clear, billowing stream from the sixteen-petalled lotus of the head, obtained forcefully through prāṇa, lives long, free from disease and with a body soft as a lotus stalk.

notes: An English subsection heading (“The Mûla Bandha”) has been removed from the verse translation; it is not part of the translated verse.
Aikya means union or oneness, not purification as in the historical English. The physiological effects are claims of the source text.
3.65.draftTranslation: Through the union of apāna and prāṇa, urine and feces diminish. Through constant mūlabandha even an old person becomes young.

notes: The historical English’s “struck dead” adds death to the simile and omits niśvasya, breathing or hissing. The Sanskrit says struck, not killed.
3.68.draftTranslation: Heated by that, the sleeping Kuṇḍalinī awakens; hissing like a she-serpent struck with a stick, she becomes straight.

notes: The historical wording obscures the inversion: this verse describes the navel/sun above the palate/moon, rather than their ordinary positions. Viparītākhā is a defective source spelling of the technique’s name.
3.79.draftTranslation: With the navel above and the palate below—the sun above and the moon below—the technique called viparītakaraṇī is learned from the teacher’s words.

notes: Sanskrit Documents has jaṭharāgnivivardhinī against GRETIL jaṭharāgni-vivardhanī. The Sinh English 79–81 divides this passage differently from GRETIL 3.80–82.
The old English includes the warning about scant food from the next Sanskrit verse. The draft now follows GRETIL’s boundary.
3.80.draftTranslation: For one continually engaged in practice it increases the digestive fire; abundant food should therefore be provided for that practitioner.

notes: Restored the warning from the first half of this verse; the instruction to increase the duration belongs to 3.82. Kṣaṇa is rendered “moment”, without equating it to a modern second.
3.81.draftTranslation: If food is scant, the fire burns at once. On the first day one should be head downward and feet upward for a moment.

notes: Restored the first half-line omitted by the historical English at this boundary. Yāma is a watch, conventionally about three hours; the historical English’s “two hours” is not adopted.
3.82.draftTranslation: One should practise a little longer than a moment each day. After six months wrinkles and grey hair are no longer seen. Whoever practises daily for a watch is said to conquer time.

notes: Corrected “free from sloth ... slothful”: nirmatsara and matsara concern freedom from envy and envy, not laziness.
3.95.draftTranslation: This yoga succeeds for the meritorious, steadfast, truth-seeing, and unenvious, but not for those filled with envy.

notes: English III.107 occurs twice verbatim in the mirror. It is imported only once; duplication is a digitization artifact, not two Sanskrit verses.

The critical edition has a related but materially different verse at 4.4 (also represented in its alternative fourth chapter). It does not license a word-for-word reconstruction of this difficult GRETIL reading. The provisional draft remains qualified, and no Sinh translation is invented.
The source’s sūrcyā- is anomalous. The surrounding sun/moon context and the critical edition’s related appended verse 4.11_9 support the draft’s interpretation; the source spelling is preserved.

The critical edition 4.57 supports bindur (binduḥ before na) where this transcription has vidur, but also differs elsewhere in the stanza. The draft’s bindu is an explicitly signalled editorial interpretation.
